q: XSS needs two things to go wrong at the same time. Which pair?
options: The server is slow, and the user picked a weak password
The site is on HTTP, and the user is on public WiFi
The page takes text from an outside source, and shows it without cleaning it first
The page loads too many scripts, and one of them fails
explain: Outside text plus no sanitizing. Once both are true, the attacker's code runs as if your own site wrote it — reading everything on the page and sending requests as the logged-in user.

q: React's JSX escapes the values you insert. Where does that protection stop?
options: Escaping is contextual: attributes, scripts and styles each follow their own rules
Only when the value is a number
explain: JSX covers plain text well. Other contexts have their own rules — an unquoted attribute can still run code like onmouseover=alert(1) even when quoting is handled correctly everywhere else.

q: You genuinely need to render raw HTML that came from a user. What do you reach for?
options: A regex that strips out <script> tags
explain: Homemade cleaners always miss a case. Sanitize by default with a vetted library, and keep CSP as the backup layer rather than the main defense.

q: What is a Content Security Policy actually for?
options: Preventing every XSS bug from ever existing
Limiting the damage if XSS does get through
Encrypting traffic between browser and server
explain: CSP tells the browser which code is allowed to run. It caps the blast radius — it does not replace sanitizing your input.

q: Why is an allowlist CSP (listing approved domains) a poor bet?
options: It is hard to maintain and breaks the moment a third-party script changes something
It noticeably slows the page down
explain: A strict CSP built on nonces or hashes holds up better, and it also blocks inline event handlers, eval(), object embeds and <base> tag hijacking.

q: What is the first step when rolling out a strict CSP?
options: Turn it on in production and see what breaks
explain: Report-Only shows what the policy would block without breaking anything. Then pick nonces or hashes, enforce for real, add strict-dynamic where scripts load scripts, and fix the inline handlers it flags.

q: Which of these should never appear in your CSP?
explain: 'unsafe-inline', data: URIs in script-src, and wildcard sources all give the policy away. default-src https: is a reasonable fallback when a strict policy is not realistic yet.

q: Your JS bundle is public. Which of these counts as information leakage?
options: Hardcoded credentials, weakly scoped API keys, and internal admin routes
explain: Anything reachable in shipped code is a free map handed to attackers. Grep production JS for secrets regularly, and make sure any exposed key is restricted by IP, referrer or API.

q: Does minifying your JavaScript hide what is inside it?
options: No — text and strings survive intact; only variable names shrink
Yes, as long as you also gzip it
Only when source maps are turned off
explain: Minifying is not hiding. Check whether file.js.map is sitting next to file.js in production, and decide on purpose whether maps ship publicly or go privately to a tool like Sentry.

q: An attacker's page makes your logged-in user's browser send a real request your user never intended. What stops it?
explain: CSRF rides the session the user already has. A token proves the request came from your own page, and SameSite stops the cookie tagging along in the first place.

q: Where should an auth token live?
options: In localStorage, so your JS can read it
In an httpOnly cookie, so JS cannot read it at all
In the URL, so it survives a refresh
explain: localStorage is readable by any script on the page, which means XSS reads it too. Cookies can be locked down with httpOnly, Secure and SameSite — localStorage has none of those.

q: The Delete button is hidden for users without permission. Is the action protected?
options: No — hiding a button is UI convenience; the server has to recheck
Yes, as long as the route is hidden too
Yes, as long as the site is on HTTPS
explain: Client-side authorization is a convenience, not a boundary. Anyone can call the endpoint directly, so permissions get rechecked on the server every time.

q: Which CORS setup is the dangerous one?
explain: A misconfigured header lets any site read data meant only for yours. Allow only trusted origins, and never mix a wildcard with credentials.

q: A user edits an ID in the URL and sees someone else's data. Where is the bug?
options: The ID should have been encrypted
The backend never rechecked permissions for that record
explain: The ID came from the user, so it cannot be trusted. The server has to confirm this user is allowed to reach that specific record.

q: Your login page accepts any URL in ?redirect=. What is the risk?
options: It can send users straight to a phishing page
It leaks the session cookie to the parameter
explain: Only redirect to a trusted allowlist. Anything else turns your own login page into the first hop of a phishing chain.

q: Most of a modern frontend is code you did not write. How does risk get in?
options: Only through packages you installed directly
Compromised packages, typosquatted names, and transitive dependencies you never chose
It does not — the registry reviews everything
explain: Dependency code runs with exactly the same trust as your own. Pin versions, use lockfiles, scan in CI, and keep the dependency list as small as the task allows.
